The genealogy of Jesus Christ (verses 1–17)

This genealogy of our Savior has a clear and necessary purpose.

It is not a pointless list of ancestors or a display of family greatness such as worldly leaders sometimes produce.

It establishes that Jesus belonged to the nation and family from which the Messiah was promised.

God promised Abraham that a blessing would come through his descendants (Genesis 12:3; 22:18).

He promised David that the kingdom would be established through his descendants.

The promises concerning Abraham's offspring and David's throne must therefore be fulfilled in one who belongs to both their families.

Henry points to 2 Samuel 7:12, Psalm 89:3 and Psalm 132:11.

Unless Jesus truly descended from David and Abraham, he could not be the promised Messiah.

Matthew establishes that descent through recognized records.

The Son of God willingly took on our human nature.

He came near to us in our fallen, miserable condition.

Yet he remained entirely free from sin.

When we read the names in his genealogy, we should remember how low the Lord of glory was willing to stoop in order to save humanity.

An angel reassures Joseph (verses 18–25)

Consider the humble circumstances in which the Son of God entered this world.

They teach us to value godliness and holiness above worldly glory and status.

The mystery of Christ becoming human should be adored rather than treated as an object of idle speculation.

He took our nature while remaining pure from the original sin that has affected Adam's descendants.

Joseph was troubled and considered what to do.

God guides thoughtful people who seriously consider their duty, not those who never reflect.

Often his instruction comes when his servants do not know what to do next.

Divine consolation is especially precious when the soul is burdened by uncertainty.

The angel announced that Mary would give birth to the Savior of the world.

Joseph was to name the child Jesus, meaning Savior, a name corresponding to Joshua.

The name describes his work.

He saves his people from their sins.

He removes sin's guilt through the merit of his death and breaks sin's power through the Spirit of his grace.

In saving them from sin, he saves them from divine wrath, the curse and every ultimate misery, both now and hereafter.

Christ came not to make people comfortable in their sins, but to rescue them from their sins.

He redeems them to belong to himself, the One set apart from sinners.

Joseph promptly and cheerfully obeyed the angel, without arguing or delaying.

In every step of life, especially during major decisions, we should seek God's direction by applying the general principles of his written word.

That is the safe and comforting course.

[Matt.1.1-Matt.1.17]
Matthew
Matthew, surnamed Levi, before his conversion was a publican, or tax-gatherer under the Romans at Capernaum. He is generally allowed to have written his Gospel before any other of the evangelists. The contents of this Gospel, and the evidence of ancient writers, show that it was written primarily for the use of the Jewish nation. The fulfilment of prophecy was regarded by the Jews as strong evidence, therefore this is especially dwelt upon by St. Matthew. Here are particularly selected such parts of our Saviour's history and discourses as were best suited to awaken the Jewish nation to a sense of their sins; to remove their erroneous expectations of an earthly kingdom; to abate their pride and self-conceit; to teach them the spiritual nature and extent of the gospel; and to prepare them for the admission of the Gentiles into the church.
Chapter 1
Chapter Outline
The genealogy of Jesus. | (1-17) |
An angel appears to Joseph. | (18-25) |
Verses 1-17
Concerning this genealogy of our Saviour, observe the chief intention. It is not a needless genealogy. It is not a vain-glorious one, as those of great men often are. It proves that our Lord Jesus is of the nation and family out of which the Messiah was to arise. The promise of the blessing was made to Abraham and his seed; of the dominion, to David and his seed. It was promised to Abraham that Christ should descend from him, [Gen.12.3] Ge 12:3; [Gen.22.18] 22:18; and to David that he should descend from him, [2Sam.7.12] 2Sa 7:12; [Ps.89.3] Psa 89:3, &c.; 132:11; and, therefore, unless Jesus is a son of David, and a son of Abraham, he is not the Messiah. Now this is here proved from well-known records. When the Son of God was pleased to take our nature, he came near to us, in our fallen, wretched condition; but he was perfectly free from sin: and while we read the names in his genealogy, we should not forget how low the Lord of glory stooped to save the human race.
[Matt.1.18-Matt.1.25]
Verses 18-25
Let us look to the circumstances under which the Son of God entered into this lower world, till we learn to despise the vain honours of this world, when compared with piety and holiness. The mystery of Christ's becoming man is to be adored, not curiously inquired into. It was so ordered that Christ should partake of our nature, yet that he should be pure from the defilement of original sin, which has been communicated to all the race of Adam. Observe, it is the thoughtful, not the unthinking, whom God will guide. God's time to come with instruction to his people, is when they are at a loss. Divine comforts most delight the soul when under the pressure of perplexed thoughts. Joseph is told that Mary should bring forth the Saviour of the world. He was to call his name Jesus, a Saviour. Jesus is the same name with Joshua. And the reason of that name is clear, for those whom Christ saves, he saves from their sins; from the guilt of sin by the merit of his death, and from the power of sin by the Spirit of his grace. In saving them from sin, he saves them from wrath and the curse, and all misery, here and hereafter. Christ came to save his people, not in their sins, but from their sins; and so to redeem them from among men, to himself, who is separate from sinners. Joseph did as the angel of the Lord had bidden him, speedily, without delay, and cheerfully, without dispute. By applying the general rules of the written word, we should in all the steps of our lives, particularly the great turns of them, take direction from God, and we shall find this safe and comfortable.

The wise men seek the newborn King (verses 1–8)

People who live far away from the usual means of grace may sometimes pursue Christ more diligently and come to know more of his salvation than those living nearby.

But no secret arts or merely human learning can bring anyone to a true knowledge of Christ.

We must learn of him through God's written word, which shines like a lamp in a dark place, and through the Holy Spirit's instruction.

When the morning star has risen in someone's heart, bringing genuine knowledge of Christ, that person desires to worship him.

Herod was old.

He had never been especially affectionate toward his own family and was unlikely to live long enough to see a newborn child grow into a political rival.

Nevertheless, he was terrified at the announcement of a new king.

He did not understand that the Messiah's kingdom was spiritual.

We must beware of lifeless faith.

A person may be convinced of many religious truths and still hate them because they challenge ambition or sinful desires.

Such a belief only increases resistance to God and his cause.

A sinner may be foolish enough to imagine that resistance will succeed.

The wise men find and worship Jesus (verses 9–12)

The wise men rejoiced when they saw the star again.

Their joy resembles that of people who have passed through a long season of temptation, spiritual darkness and fear and then receive the Spirit of adoption.

That Spirit witnesses with their spirits that they are children of God.

They may have been surprised when they found a cottage instead of a palace, and a poor mother instead of royal attendants.

But they did not turn away.

They had found the King they sought and gladly gave him their gifts.

Sincere seekers of Christ will not be disappointed because they find him and his followers in obscure places rather than among wealth and power.

Perhaps someone wants to worship Christ but thinks, “I am poor and foolish, and I have nothing to offer him.”

You still have your heart, though it is unworthy, hard and unclean.

Give it to Christ as it is.

Be willing for him to use and change it as he pleases.

He will receive it, make it better, shape it in his likeness and give you himself forever.

The wise men offered gold, frankincense and myrrh.

Providence had sent these gifts as timely help for Joseph and Mary, who were poor.

Our heavenly Father knows what his children need.

He can appoint one person to provide for another and bring support even from the ends of the earth.

Joseph takes the family to Egypt (verses 13–15)

Egypt had once been the place of Israel's slavery and had been particularly cruel to Israelite infants.

Now God made it a refuge for the holy child Jesus.

The Lord can use even the worst places for the best purposes.

This journey tested the faith of Joseph and Mary.

Their faith was tested and proved firm.

Whenever we or our young children experience danger and hardship, let us remember the difficulties Christ himself faced as an infant.

Herod kills the children of Bethlehem (verses 16–18)

Herod ordered the murder of the young boys in Bethlehem and its surrounding villages.

Uncontrolled anger, backed by illegitimate power, can lead to almost unimaginable cruelty.

Henry writes that God was not unjust in permitting these events, because fallen human beings' lives are subject to divine judgment from the beginning.

He relates the deaths and diseases of young children to original sin.

These are Henry's theological explanations of divine permission; they do not excuse Herod's murder.

Henry calls the children's deaths their martyrdom.

How early persecution against Christ and his kingdom began!

Herod may have believed he had frustrated the Old Testament prophecies and defeated the wise men's search.

But whatever cunning and cruelty human beings devise, the Lord's purpose will stand.

Jesus returns and lives in Nazareth (verses 19–23)

Egypt could serve as a temporary place of refuge, but not as the family's permanent home.

Christ was sent to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, so he was to return to them.

If we regarded this present world as our Egypt, a place of temporary exile and bondage, and heaven as our Canaan, our true home and rest, we would depart just as readily when the Lord calls us.

Joseph brought the family to Galilee.

They settled in Nazareth, a town people regarded with contempt.

The name Nazarene was later used as an accusation against Christ.

Wherever Providence assigns us to live, we should be prepared to share the disgrace Christ experienced.

Yet we may gladly bear his name, knowing that if we suffer with him, we will also be glorified with him.

Egypt may serve to sojourn in, or take shelter in, for awhile, but not to abide in. Christ was sent to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, to them he must return. He began his public ministry in the wilderness of Judea, an area not densely populated or extensively settled, rather than an entirely uninhabited desert.

No place is so remote that divine grace cannot reach it.

The word means a comprehensive change of mind: a new understanding, disposition, set of affections and direction for the soul.

Consider your ways.

You have thought wrongly; think again, and think rightly.

True repentance changes how we think about God and Christ, about sin and holiness, and about this life and eternity.

A change of mind produces a changed way of living.

Gospel repentance springs from seeing Christ, recognizing his love and hoping for pardon through him.

We are invited to repent because God promises forgiveness to those who do.

Turn toward him through obedience, and through Christ he receives you in mercy.

Repentance and humility are still necessary if a person is to welcome the Lord.

To prepare a soul for Christ, much spiritual work is needed.

The ways of Satan and sin are crooked.

The path prepared for Christ must be made straight (Hebrews 12:13).

The secondary witness also includes a reference to Zechariah 13:1 at this point; the exact original-native placement and relevance of that reference require verification, rather than silent correction.

John warns the Pharisees and Sadducees (verses 7–12)

A sermon comes alive when its truths are applied directly to the consciences of the listeners.

John did this.

The Pharisees chiefly relied upon outward forms of religion, neglecting the weightier requirements of the moral law and the spiritual meaning of ceremonies.

Some were outright hypocrites who used a pretense of holiness as a covering for wrongdoing.

The Sadducees took the opposite extreme: they denied spirits and a future state, showing contempt for the truths others professed.

There is a coming wrath, and everyone needs to flee from it.

God does not delight in human ruin.

He warns through the written word, ministers and conscience.

People who say they regret their sins but continue deliberately committing them do not possess genuine repentance.

True penitents are humble, grateful for small mercies, patient under great suffering, watchful against every appearance of sin, faithful in their duties and charitable toward others.

We must not trust in external religious privileges.

The human heart can invent many excuses to evade the convincing and commanding power of God's word.

Many people rest on church membership and outward honors but never enter heaven.

The warning is meant to awaken the careless.

Only the regenerating Spirit of Christ can make a corrupt heart produce good fruit.

Every tree without fruit appropriate to repentance will eventually be cut down and cast into judgment, regardless of its outward gifts, reputation or impressive appearance.

If a tree does not produce fruit, it is fit only for fuel.

John's preaching also announced the purpose of the Messiah's arrival.

No outward ordinance, no matter who administers it or by what method, can replace the baptism of the Holy Spirit and fire.

Only the Spirit's cleansing power can make a heart pure and produce the holy affections that accompany salvation.

He also grants the Spirit's graces and comforts to those who ask him (Luke 11:13; John 7:38–39; Acts 11:16).

The secondary witness prints a reference to Isaiah 21:10 near this statement; its original source context should be checked separately, without altering the pinned module.

Believers are like wheat—substantial, useful and precious.

Hypocrites are like chaff—empty and easily blown about.

They are presently mixed within the same outward religious community.

But the final judgment will separate them completely.

In heaven, believers will be gathered safely, free from corrupt neighbors and from the remaining corruption within their own hearts.

There will be no chaff among them.

Hell is the unquenchable fire that awaits impenitent unbelief and hypocrisy.

Life and death, good and evil, are set before us.

How we stand before God now determines which side of the final separation we will enter.

Jesus is baptized by John (verses 13–17)

The humility and kindness of Christ are so extraordinary that even mature believers may initially struggle to understand them.

Even people who know his will may raise objections to his way of acting.

Those who have received much of God's Spirit should recognize their continued need to seek more grace from Christ.

Jesus did not deny that John needed the baptism Christ could give.

Yet Jesus insisted that John should now baptize him, because the Savior had entered a state of humiliation.

It was appropriate for him to fulfill all righteousness.

He acknowledged every divine institution and willingly obeyed God's righteous commands.

Through Christ, heaven is opened to sinful humanity.

The Spirit produces love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control.

After Malachi there was no prophet until John the Baptist came. He appeared first in the wilderness of Judea. This was not an uninhabited desert, but a part of the country not thickly peopled, nor much enclosed. No place is so remote as to shut us out from the visits of Divine grace. The doctrine he preached was repentance; "Repent ye." The word here used, implies a total alteration in the mind, a change in the judgment, disposition, and affections, another and a better bias of the soul. Consider your ways, change your minds: you have thought amiss; think again, and think aright. True penitents have other thoughts of God and Christ, sin and holiness, of this world and the other, than they had. The change of the mind produces a change of the way. That is gospel repentance, which flows from a sight of Christ, from a sense of his love, and from hopes of pardon and forgiveness through him. It is a great encouragement to us to repent; repent, for your sins shall be pardoned upon your repentance. Return to God in a way of duty, and he will, through Christ, return unto you in the way of mercy. It is still as necessary to repent and humble ourselves, to prepare the way of the Lord, as it then was. There is a great deal to be done, to make way for Christ into a soul, and nothing is more needful than the discovery of sin, and a conviction that we cannot be saved by our own righteousness. By giving others this example, John made way for Christ. Many came to John's baptism, but few kept to the profession they made. There may be many forward hearers, where there are few true believers. Curiosity, and love for novelty and variety, may bring many to attend on good preaching, and to be affected for a while, who never are subject to the power of it. Those who received John's doctrine, testified their repentance by confessing their sins. Those only are ready to receive Jesus Christ as their righteousness, who are brought with sorrow and shame to own their guilt. The benefits of the kingdom of heaven, now at hand, were thereupon sealed to them by baptism. John washed them with water, in token that God would cleanse them from all their iniquities, thereby intimating, that by nature and practice all were polluted, and could not be admitted among the people of God, unless washed from their sins in the fountain Christ was to open, [Zech.13.1] Zec 13:1.
[Matt.3.7-Matt.3.12]

The Pharisees laid their chief stress on outward observances, neglecting the weightier matters of the moral law, and the spiritual meaning of their legal ceremonies. They were the scornful infidels of that time and country. There is a wrath to come. It is the great concern of every one to flee from that wrath. Immediately after Jesus was declared to be the Son of God and the Savior of the world, he was tempted.

But Jesus had no corrupt nature, and therefore his temptation came from the devil, not from inward sinful desire.

Satan is subtle, malicious and daring, but he can be resisted.

Christ's experience comforts us: being tempted is not itself sin when the temptation is refused.

In that case it is suffering, not guilt.

Satan's aim in every temptation was to lead Christ into sin against God.

First, he tempted Jesus to distrust his Father's goodness and care.

Satan often attacks when outward circumstances are difficult.

People in distress must be especially watchful.

Jesus answered the devil by appealing to what Scripture says.

This is our example.

No need, however pressing, gives us permission to use sinful means of providing for ourselves.

The Lord can and will provide through the means he appoints.

Both despair and presumption are extremely dangerous, especially in spiritual matters.

Satan has no objection to attacking us in holy places.

Those who rise high can become especially exposed to the enemy's assaults.

Satan knew enough Scripture to quote it.

Satan omitted part of the promise he quoted.

Stepping outside our duty forfeits any claim that the promise authorizes our recklessness.

God's promises remain firm, but they do not authorize us to continue in sin so that grace may increase.

Worldly splendor is one of the most attractive traps for careless people.

Some temptations are so obviously wicked that we must not deliberate over them, but reject them immediately.

When the devil is resisted, he flees.

A heart that pauses to negotiate is almost defeated.

What can anyone gain by possessing the whole world while losing their soul?

After the temptation, Christ received help and comfort.

This encouraged him in his mission and encourages us to trust him.

He knows from experience what it is to suffer temptation and receive timely help.

Therefore he not only sympathizes with tempted believers but comes to their aid when they need it.

God acts justly in withdrawing the gospel and opportunities for grace from people who despise them and push them away.

Christ will not remain where he is unwelcome.

People without him live in darkness.

They may even sit contentedly in it, choosing ignorance rather than light.

When the gospel enters a place or a human heart, it is like the arrival of daylight.

Light reveals what is hidden and shows the way forward; so does the gospel.

Repentance belongs to gospel preaching.

Not only the strict John the Baptist but also the gracious Jesus himself proclaimed repentance.

When Jesus began preaching, he also began gathering disciples.

They would first hear his teaching and later preach it.

They would witness his miracles and afterward testify to them.

He went not to Herod's court or to the chief priests and elders in Jerusalem, but to fishermen beside the Sea of Galilee.

The power that called Peter and Andrew could also have converted Annas and Caiaphas, because nothing is impossible with God.

But Christ chose those considered foolish by the world to put worldly wisdom to shame.

Diligence in honest work pleases Christ and does not hinder holiness.

Idleness exposes people more readily to Satan's temptations than to God's call.

It is encouraging to see young people caring for their parents and fulfilling their duties.

Paralysis was extreme bodily weakness.

Lunacy, as Henry's historical term, described severe disorder of the mind.

Demonic possession was an affliction involving both bodily and mental misery.

Christ healed all three.

By restoring bodily health, he showed that his greatest mission was to cure the diseases of the soul.

Sin is the soul's sickness, suffering and torment.

Jesus came to take away sin and heal the soul.

Jesus teaches his disciples (verses 1 and 2)

No one can find true happiness in this life or in the next without seeking it from Christ, according to the teaching of his word.

He showed his listeners which evils they should hate and which good things they should eagerly seek and practice.

The eight blessings (verses 3–12)

Our Savior described eight kinds of blessed people.

Together, they show the principal graces that should characterize Christians.

First, the poor in spirit are blessed.

Such people respond humbly to humble circumstances.

They are lowly in their own estimation.

They recognize their spiritual need, grieve over their guilt and eagerly desire a Redeemer.

The kingdom of grace belongs to them now, and the kingdom of glory awaits them.

Second, those who mourn are blessed.

This is godly sorrow that produces sincere repentance, watchfulness, humility and continual dependence on God's mercy through Jesus Christ.

It also leads people to seek the Holy Spirit's continuing work of cleansing away sin.

Heaven is the Lord's mountain of joy, but our path toward it passes through a valley of tears.

God himself will comfort those who mourn in this way.

Third, the meek are blessed.

Meek people quietly submit to God, bear insults without retaliation and respond gently or remain silent when appropriate.

Through patience they maintain possession of their own souls, even when they can scarcely hold on to anything else.

Meekness often promotes comfort, safety and even outward well-being in this life.

Fourth, those who hunger and thirst for righteousness are blessed.

Here righteousness represents all spiritual blessings.

These blessings were purchased through Christ's righteousness and are assured by God's faithfulness.

We should desire them as earnestly as hungry and thirsty people desire food and water.

Not every desire for grace is itself a work of grace.

But this kind of spiritual longing is created by God, who will not abandon the work of his hands.

Fifth, the merciful are blessed.

We must not merely endure our own suffering patiently.

We should do everything possible to relieve other people's misery.

We must care for their souls as well as their circumstances, pitying those trapped in sin and seeking to rescue them like burning brands pulled from the fire.

Sixth, the pure in heart are blessed, for they will see God.

Holiness and happiness are united in this blessing.

Our hearts must be purified through faith and reserved for the Lord.

Let us pray, “Create a clean heart in me, O God.”

Only the pure are able to see God and rejoice in his holiness.

Heaven would not be happiness to an impure heart.

As God cannot approve sin, those determined to remain in sin cannot delight in his purity.

Seventh, the peacemakers are blessed.

They love peace, seek it and work to remain quiet and respectful.

They protect peace from being broken and seek to restore it when it has been lost.

If those who make peace are blessed, woe to those who break it.

Eighth, those who are persecuted for righteousness are blessed.

This blessing is especially characteristic of Christianity and receives more explanation than the others.

There is nothing about suffering that earns merit before God.

Yet God will ensure that those who lose anything for his sake—even life itself—will not finally lose by serving him.

How different Christ's teaching is from the world's!

The world admires the proud, fashionable, rich, powerful and victorious.

May the Lord show us mercy, acknowledge us as his children and bring us into his kingdom.

With that hope, we can face humble or painful circumstances with joy.

Salt and light (verses 13–16)

Humanity, lying in ignorance and evil, resembled a vast heap ready to decay.

Christ sent his disciples to act as salt, preserving and seasoning the world through their teaching and way of life.

If they fail in that calling, they become like salt that has lost its flavor.

A person may profess Christ while remaining without grace.

No other message or means can make that person useful apart from true saving change.

Our light must shine through good works visible to other people.

What passes privately between God and our souls should remain private.

But conduct that is naturally public should match our Christian profession and be worthy of respect.

Our goal must always be God's glory, not our own reputation.

Christ fulfills and confirms God's law (verses 17–20)

No one should imagine that Christ allows his people to take God's holy law lightly.

No sinner participates in Christ's justifying righteousness without repentance.

The mercy announced by the gospel makes a believer more deeply aware of sin, not less.

God's law becomes the Christian's guide for duty, in which the believer delights.

Anyone who deliberately permits disobedience while claiming to follow Christ—or teaches others to do so—cannot be a genuine disciple, regardless of public status.

Everyone entering God's kingdom needs Christ's righteousness imputed through faith alone.

But a renewed heart also produces a comprehensive change in attitudes and actions.

Anger and reconciliation: the sixth commandment (verses 21–26)

Some Jewish teachers had reduced the command against murder to a prohibition of the outward act of killing.

They had neglected its spiritual meaning.

Christ revealed the command's true scope, by which we will be judged and should therefore live.

Reckless anger is murder in the heart.

Our brother or neighbor includes every human being, however lowly their station, because all people were made of one blood.

“Raca” expresses contempt flowing from pride.

“You fool”, used spitefully, expresses hatred.

Malicious slander and condemnation are like slow, secret poison.

Christ warns that what people dismiss as trivial will be brought before God's judgment.

We must protect Christian love and seek peace with everyone.

If we have injured another person, we should confess wrongdoing, humble ourselves and make or offer appropriate amends, whether the harm was done by speech or conduct.

We should do so promptly.

Unreconciled hostility hinders our fitness to participate in holy worship.

Preparing for worship provides a fitting opportunity for self-examination.

This also teaches our need to be reconciled to God through Christ.

While we live, we are still on our way to his judgment seat.

After death it will be too late.

Because life is uncertain and the matter is so serious, we must seek peace with God without delay.

Purity and fidelity: the seventh commandment (verses 27–32)

Victory over corrupt inward desires may require painful struggle.

Yet it must be pursued.

Every spiritual resource has been given to save us from sin, not to keep us comfortable in it.

Every sense and ability should be guarded against occasions of wrongdoing.

Those who lead others toward temptation, including through deliberately provocative appearance or other behavior, bear responsibility for their influence.

People accept painful medical treatments to preserve bodily life.

What should they be willing to endure to protect the eternal welfare of their souls?

God's commands are expressions of tender mercy.

His Spirit supplies the grace and consolation needed to obey them.

Truthfulness and oaths: the third commandment (verses 33–37)

Henry does not understand Christ to forbid every solemn oath.

Oaths taken in court or on other proper occasions may be lawful when made reverently and truthfully.

But oaths used needlessly in ordinary conversation are sinful.

So are verbal formulas intended to escape the responsibility of swearing truthfully while still pretending to invoke God.

The more dishonest people become, the less an oath restrains them.

The more truthful people become, the less they need oaths to be believed.

Christ does not prescribe exact words to use in every affirmation or denial.

He requires consistent truthfulness, making unnecessary oaths needless.

Refusing retaliation (verses 38–42)

We should be willing to endure injuries that can rightly be borne for the sake of peace, entrusting our affairs to the Lord.

Christians should avoid needless quarrels and fighting.

Someone may object that human nature cannot endure an insult without answering it.

But flesh and blood cannot inherit God's kingdom.

Those governed by right principles will enjoy more peace and comfort than those ruled by offended pride.

Love even your enemies (verses 43–48)

Some Jewish teachers interpreted “neighbor” as referring only to people of their own nation, religion or group, whom they already regarded as friends.

Jesus commands genuine kindness toward everyone.

We should especially care for other people's souls.

We must pray for our enemies.

Many people return kindness for kindness.

Christ calls his disciples to return good for evil.

That reveals a nobler principle than the ordinary conduct of the world.

Others greet and embrace only people from their own party or opinion.

We must not limit our respect so narrowly.

Christians ought to desire and pursue maturity and completeness in grace and holiness, following the example of the heavenly Father (1 Peter 1:15–16).

More is rightly expected from Christ's followers than from others.

Let us ask God to enable us to show, through our lives, that we truly are his children.

Giving without hypocrisy (verses 1–4)

Our Lord warned his followers against hypocrisy and outward display in religious duties. What we do must arise from an inward principle and aim at God's approval, not people's praise.

Giving to the needy is good and necessary. The fact that hypocrites misuse it to promote themselves does not lessen its value.

Vanity is subtle. We can begin seeking admiration before we even notice the temptation.

Jesus said that those who give in order to be seen already have their reward: people see them. That is all they wanted, and it is a miserable reward compared with God's promise.

The less we dwell upon our good deeds, the more fully God notices them.

He rewards not as an employer paying a worker no more than the wages earned, but as a Father generously blessing his child.

Praying without hypocrisy (verses 5–8)

Jesus assumed his disciples would pray. Finding a living Christian who never prays would be as unnatural as finding a living person who never breathes.

Prayerlessness betrays gracelessness.

The scribes and Pharisees fell into two errors: seeking human admiration and using empty repetitions.

If our prayers, in which we approach God about matters of eternal importance, are made for the sake of people's praise, it is just that praise should be our only reward.

God hears even a brief, silent longing directed toward him.

His answer is a gift of grace, not a debt; there is no human merit in asking for help.

When he does not grant exactly what his people request, it is because he knows the gift is not needed or would not be good for them.

The length and wording of a prayer do not manipulate him. Some of the strongest intercessions come through groanings too deep for words.

Let us learn daily from Christ how to pray, with the right disposition of heart.

Jesus teaches us how to pray (verses 9–15)

The Lord's Prayer teaches both the subjects and the order of Christian prayer.

We are not restricted to reciting this prayer alone, or required to recite it every time. Yet using it is good, provided we understand what we say and do not repeat it without purpose.

It contains much in few words.

Its six petitions are arranged meaningfully: the first three focus especially on God's honor, and the final three concern our temporal and spiritual needs.

We seek God's kingdom and righteousness first. Only after praying for his name, kingdom and will do we ask for the support and comforts required in earthly life.

Every word teaches something.

Bread teaches moderation. We ask for what we need, rather than every luxury we might desire.

Our bread teaches honesty and diligence. We do not ask for another person's bread, or bread gained through deception (Proverbs 20:17), or through idleness (Proverbs 31:27). We seek what is honestly earned.

Daily bread teaches continual dependence upon God's Providence.

We ask him to give it, not to sell or lend it. Even the greatest people depend upon his mercy for everyday food.

We say give us, not merely give me. We must care for the poor and pray with and for our families.

We ask for it today. Just as our bodies need daily food, our souls should daily renew their desire for God. We need prayer as surely as bread.

The prayer also teaches us to hate and fear sin while hoping for mercy. We must distrust our own strength, depend on God's protecting grace, prepare to resist the tempter and avoid tempting others.

Jesus promises that those who forgive others will receive their heavenly Father's forgiveness. We must show mercy if we hope to receive it.

Christ came not only to reconcile sinners to God, but also to reconcile them to one another.

Fasting without display (verses 16–18)

Religious fasting is a duty of Christ's disciples. Yet it is principally a means of preparing the heart for other duties, not a performance with value merely in itself.

Fasting expresses the humbling of the soul (Psalm 35:13). That inward reality must be our chief concern.

Do not seek public recognition for its outward appearance.

God sees what is done in secret and will reward it openly.

Treasures, spiritual sight and masters (verses 19–24)

Worldliness is a common and deadly sign of hypocrisy.

Few things allow Satan to hold the heart more firmly while a person still maintains an outward religious profession.

Every soul looks for something to treasure above all else—something in which it places its happiness, confidence and delight.

Christ directs us toward the invisible, eternal treasures of heaven.

Through Jesus Christ we should make every effort to be sure of our interest in eternal life. Nothing earthly can compare with its incorruptible inheritance, secure beyond the changes of time.

A worldly person begins with a false principle about what matters most; therefore, the thoughts and decisions built upon that principle also go wrong.

The teaching about the eye and light also applies to false religion. A person may call something light that is actually deep darkness.

We should therefore test the principles guiding our lives by God's word, praying earnestly for the Spirit's instruction.

A person may perform occasional tasks for two employers but cannot devote the heart entirely to two masters.

God requires the whole heart. He does not share it with the world.

When their demands conflict, one master must be chosen.

Whoever clings to the world as the supreme good will despise God. Whoever loves God must renounce the world's friendship.

Trusting God's fatherly care (verses 25–34)

Our Lord repeatedly warned his disciples against anxious, distracting and distrustful concern about everyday needs.

The poor may fall into this temptation just as easily as the wealthy fall into love of riches.

There is also a proper and necessary care for earthly duties. Jesus did not abolish that responsibility; he warned against carrying it into unbelieving anxiety.

Entrust the length of your life to God. Our times are in his hands, and his hands are good.

Entrust life's pleasures and hardships to him as well. He knows whether to make our circumstances sweet or bitter.

God has promised food and clothing; we may therefore look to him for them without being anxious over next year, old age or what we shall leave behind.

We should neither boast about tomorrow nor torment ourselves over tomorrow.

The One who gave us life and our bodies is surely able to supply the lesser necessities that sustain them.

If we attend to our souls and to eternity, we may trust him for food and clothing.

We must learn to accept the condition Providence has assigned us, just as we accept our physical stature. Worry cannot change his plans.

Concern for our souls is the best remedy for consuming concern about worldly things.

Seek first God's kingdom. Do not imagine that pursuing true religion will cause us to starve; God knows how to supply his people even in this present life.

Through daily prayer we receive strength for daily troubles and resistance to their temptations.

Happy are those who trust themselves entirely to God's wise care. May the Spirit expose our lack of trust and remove the worldliness remaining in our hearts.

In these verses we are cautioned against hypocrisy in giving alms. Take heed of it. It is a subtle sin; and vain-glory creeps into what we do, before we are aware. But the duty is not the less necessary and excellent for being abused by hypocrites to serve their pride. The doom Christ passes, at first may seem a promise, but it is their reward; not the reward God promises to those who do good, but the reward hypocrites promise themselves, and a poor reward it is; they did it to be seen of men, and they are seen of men. When we take least notice of our good deeds ourselves, God takes most notice of them. He will reward thee; not as a master who gives his servant what he earns, and no more, but as a Father who gives abundantly to his son that serves him.
[Matt.6.5-Matt.6.8]
Verses 5-8
It is taken for granted that all who are disciples of Christ pray. You may as soon find a living man that does not breathe, as a living Christian that does not pray. If prayerless, then graceless. The Scribes and Pharisees were guilty of two great faults in prayer, vain-glory and vain repetitions. "Verily they have their reward;" if in so great a matter as is between us and God, when we are at prayer, we can look to so poor a thing as the praise of men, it is just that it should be all our reward. Yet there is not a secret, sudden breathing after God, but he observes it. It is called a reward, but it is of grace, not of debt; what merit can there be in begging? If he does not give his people what they ask, it is because he knows they do not need it, and that it is not for their good. So far is God from being wrought upon by the length or words of our prayers, that the most powerful intercessions are those which are made with groanings that cannot be uttered. Let us well study what is shown of the frame of mind in which our prayers should be offered, and learn daily from Christ how to pray.
[Matt.6.9-Matt.6.15]
Verses 9-15
Christ saw it needful to show his disciples what must commonly be the matter and method of their prayer. Not that we are tied up to the use of this only, or of this always; yet, without doubt, it is very good to use it. It has much in a little; and it is used acceptably no further than it is used with understanding, and without being needlessly repeated. The petitions are six; the first three relate more expressly to God and his honour, the last three to our own concerns, both temporal and spiritual. This prayer teaches us to seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and that all other things shall be added. After the things of God's glory, kingdom, and will, we pray for the needful supports and comforts of this present life. Every word here has a lesson in it. We ask for bread; that teaches us sobriety and temperance: and we ask only for bread; not for what we do not need. We ask for our bread; that teaches us honesty and industry: we do not ask for the bread of others, nor the bread of deceit, [Prov.20.17] Pr 20:17; nor the bread of idleness, [Prov.31.27] Pr 31:27, but the bread honestly gotten. We ask for our daily bread; which teaches us constantly to depend upon Divine Providence. We beg of God to give it us; not sell it us, nor lend it us, but give it. The greatest of men must be beholden to the mercy of God for their daily bread. We pray, Give it to us. This teaches us a compassion for the poor. Also that we ought to pray with our families. We pray that God would give it us this day; which teaches us to renew the desires of our souls toward God, as the wants of our bodies are renewed. As the day comes we must pray to our heavenly Father, and reckon we could as well go a day without food, as without prayer. We are taught to hate and dread sin while we hope for mercy, to distrust ourselves, to rely on the providence and grace of God to keep us from it, to be prepared to resist the tempter, and not to become tempters of others. Here is a promise, If you forgive, your heavenly Father will also forgive. We must forgive, as we hope to be forgiven. Those who desire to find mercy with God, must show mercy to their brethren. Christ came into the world as the great Peace-maker, not only to reconcile us to God, but one to another.
[Matt.6.16-Matt.6.18]
Verses 16-18
Religious fasting is a duty required of the disciples of Christ, but it is not so much a duty itself, as a means to dispose us for other duties. Fasting is the humbling of the soul, [Ps.35.13] Psa 35:13; that is the inside of the duty; let that, therefore, be thy principal care, and as to the outside of it, covet not to let it be seen. God sees in secret, and will reward openly.
[Matt.6.19-Matt.6.24]
Verses 19-24
Worldly-mindedness is a common and fatal symptom of hypocrisy, for by no sin can Satan have a surer and faster hold of the soul, under the cloak of a profession of religion. Something the soul will have, which it looks upon as the best thing; in which it has pleasure and confidence above other things. Christ counsels to make our best things the joys and glories of the other world, those things not seen which are eternal, and to place our happiness in them. There are treasures in heaven. It is our wisdom to give all diligence to make our title to eternal life sure through Jesus Christ, and to look on all things here below, as not worthy to be compared with it, and to be content with nothing short of it. It is happiness above and beyond the changes and chances of time, an inheritance incorruptible. The worldly man is wrong in his first principle; therefore all his reasonings and actions therefrom must be wrong. It is equally to be applied to false religion; that which is deemed light is thick darkness. This is an awful, but a common case; we should therefore carefully examine our leading principles by the word of God, with earnest prayer for the teaching of his Spirit. A man may do some service to two masters, but he can devote himself to the service of no more than one. God requires the whole heart, and will not share it with the world. When two masters oppose each other, no man can serve both. He who holds to the world and loves it, must despise God; he who loves God, must give up the friendship of the world.
[Matt.6.25-Matt.6.34]
Verses 25-34
There is scarcely any sin against which our Lord Jesus more warns his disciples, than disquieting, distracting, distrustful cares about the things of this life. This often insnares the poor as much as the love of wealth does the rich. But there is a carefulness about temporal things which is a duty, though we must not carry these lawful cares too far. Take no thought for your life. Not about the length of it; but refer it to God to lengthen or shorten it as he pleases; our times are in his hand, and they are in a good hand. Not about the comforts of this life; but leave it to God to make it bitter or sweet as he pleases. Food and raiment God has promised, therefore we may expect them. Take no thought for the morrow, for the time to come. Be not anxious for the future, how you shall live next year, or when you are old, or what you shall leave behind you. As we must not boast of tomorrow, so we must not care for to-morrow, or the events of it. God has given us life, and has given us the body. And what can he not do for us, who did that? If we take care about our souls and for eternity, which are more than the body and its life, we may leave it to God to provide for us food and raiment, which are less. Improve this as an encouragement to trust in God. We must reconcile ourselves to our worldly estate, as we do to our stature. We cannot alter the disposals of Providence, therefore we must submit and resign ourselves to them. Thoughtfulness for our souls is the best cure of thoughtfulness for the world. Seek first the kingdom of God, and make religion your business: say not that this is the way to starve; no, it is the way to be well provided for, even in this world. The conclusion of the whole matter is, that it is the will and command of the Lord Jesus, that by daily prayers we may get strength to bear us up under our daily troubles, and to arm us against the temptations that attend them, and then let none of these things move us. Happy are those who take the Lord for their God, and make full proof of it by trusting themselves wholly to his wise disposal. Let thy Spirit convince us of sin in the want of this disposition, and take away the worldliness of our hearts.

This does not mean any sin is harmless. Even a tiny splinter in an eye or a gnat in a throat causes pain and danger and must be removed.

Charity may teach us to describe our brother's fault as a small splinter; true repentance and godly grief should make us regard our own sin as a large beam.

It is astonishing that people can live in a sinful and miserable condition without noticing it, just as it would be astonishing to overlook a beam lodged in one's eye.

The god of this world blinds human minds.

The first rule for anyone seeking to correct another person is therefore to reform oneself first.

Asking, seeking and knocking (verses 7–11)

Prayer is the appointed means of obtaining what we need.

Pray often, seriously and earnestly.

Ask like a beggar asking for help or a traveler asking for directions.

Seek like someone searching for a lost treasure or a merchant searching for precious pearls.

Knock like someone who longs to enter a house. Sin has shut and barred the door against us; through prayer we knock.

God grants what is requested according to his promises when he knows it is fitting for us. What more could we rightly desire?

The invitation extends to everyone who prays in faith: Jews and Gentiles, young and old, rich and poor, people of high or low standing, masters and servants, educated and uneducated.

All are equally welcome at the throne of grace.

Parents, though sometimes unwisely indulgent, generally wish to give good gifts to their children.

Our heavenly Father is perfectly wise. He knows what we need and what is truly good for us.

He would never command us to pray only to refuse to hear us—or to give us what would harm us.

Treating others well and choosing the narrow way (verses 12–14)

Christ came to teach us not merely what to know and believe, but what to do.

His instruction governs relationships with God and with everyone else—not only people who share our convictions or belong to our own party.

We should put ourselves in our neighbor's position and treat that person as we recognize it would be reasonable and right for us to be treated.

Jesus then described two ways, the right and the wrong, leading to eternal life and destruction.

There is no third destination in the life to come and no middle path in the present one.

The gate of sin is wide and already open. People can enter it without denying their sinful appetites or passions.

The road beyond it is broad and contains many different kinds of wrongdoing; it is crowded.

Yet why should anyone willingly go to destruction with a crowd rather than accept eternal life without that crowd?

The way to life is narrow.

Passing through the narrow gate does not mean our journey is finished. Self must be denied, the body disciplined and corrupt desires put to death.

Daily temptations must be resisted and duties performed. We must remain watchful through many troubles.

Still, this way is inviting because it leads both to the present joy of God's favor and to eternal blessedness.

That hope makes the hardships bearable.

People in every age have tried to explain away Christ's clear teaching.

True disciples are often regarded as unusual or unfashionable, while those who follow the majority continue on the broad road.

When we hear of the narrow gate and the few who find it, should we not ask whether we ourselves have entered and how faithfully we are continuing?

Few things prevent people from entering the narrow gate more effectively than flattering, flesh-pleasing teaching that contradicts the truth.

Such teachers are known by the tendency and effects of their doctrine.

Some aspect of their character and conduct will conflict with Christ's teaching.

A religious opinion that leads people into sin does not come from God.

Calling Christ our Master with our lips is not enough.

We must believe in him, repent of sin, live a holy life and love one another.

Our sanctification is God's will.

Everyone who names Christ must turn away from sin.

Those who work for Christ can be encouraged that his work will certainly be accomplished.

God's Providence extends to all his creatures, even the smallest sparrows.

His people are worth more than many sparrows.

Even the hairs on their heads are numbered. The Lord knows and cares for each person who belongs to him.

We must not merely believe in Christ in private.

When called to do so, we must confess him openly, even under persecution.

Henry qualifies the warning about denial: it concerns a denial persisted in.

The promised reward of confession likewise belongs to confession that truly and consistently arises from faith and love.

Religion is worth more than everything else.

Everyone who really knows its value will be willing to surrender competing interests for it.

Christ leads his people through suffering into glory.

Those least attached to earthly life are best prepared for the life to come.

Even a small kindness shown to one of Christ's disciples is accepted when it is all a person has the opportunity and ability to offer.

But such kindness does not earn a claim against God.

We can merit nothing from his hand.

Any reward is a free gift of grace.

Let us confess Christ courageously and demonstrate love for him in everything.

[Matt.10.1-Matt.10.4]
Chapter 10
Chapter Outline
The apostles called. | (1-4) |
The apostles instructed and sent forth. | (5-15) |
Directions to the apostles. | (16-42) |
Verses 1-4
The word "apostle" signifies messenger; they were Christ's messengers, sent forth to proclaim his kingdom. Christ gave them power to heal all manner of sickness. In the grace of the gospel there is a slave for every sore, a remedy for every malady. There is no spiritual disease, but there is power in Christ for the cure of it. There names are recorded, and it is their honour; yet they had more reason to rejoice that their names were written in heaven, while the high and mighty names of the great ones of the earth are buried in the dust.
[Matt.10.5-Matt.10.15]
Verses 5-15
The Gentiles must not have the gospel brought them, till the Jews have refused it. This restraint on the apostles was only in their first mission. Wherever they went they must proclaim, The kingdom of heaven is at hand. They preached, to establish the faith; the kingdom, to animate the hope; of heaven, to inspire the love of heavenly things, and the contempt of earthly; which is at hand, that men may prepare for it without delay. Christ gave power to work miracles for the confirming of their doctrine. This is not necessary now that the kingdom of God is come. It showed that the intent of the doctrine they preached, was to heal sick souls, and to raise those that were dead in sin. In proclaiming the gospel of free grace for the healing and saving of men's souls, we must above all avoid the appearance of the spirit of an hireling. They are directed what to do in strange towns and cities. The servant of Christ is the ambassador of peace to whatever place he is sent. His message is even to the vilest sinners, yet it behoves him to find out the best persons in every place. It becomes us to pray heartily for all, and to conduct ourselves courteously to all. They are directed how to act as to those that refused them. The whole counsel of God must be declared, and those who will not attend to the gracious message, must be shown that their state is dangerous. This should be seriously laid to heart by all that hear the gospel, lest their privileges only serve to increase their condemnation.
[Matt.10.16-Matt.10.42]
Verses 16-42
Our Lord warned his disciples to prepare for persecution. They were to avoid all things which gave advantage to their enemies, all meddling with worldly or political concerns, all appearance of evil or selfishness, and all underhand measures. Christ foretold troubles, not only that the troubles might not be a surprise, but that they might confirm their faith. He tells them what they should suffer, and from whom. Thus Christ has dealt fairly and faithfully with us, in telling us the worst we can meet with in his service; and he would have us deal so with ourselves, in sitting down and counting the cost. Persecutors are worse than beasts, in that they prey upon those of their own kind. The strongest bonds of love and duty, have often been broken through from enmity against Christ. Sufferings from friends and relations are very grievous; nothing cuts more. It appears plainly, that all who will live godly in Christ Jesus must suffer persecution; and we must expect to enter into the kingdom of God through many tribulations. With these predictions of trouble, are counsels and comforts for a time of trial. The disciples of Christ are hated and persecuted as serpents, and their ruin is sought, and they need the serpent's wisdom. Be ye harmless as doves. Not only, do nobody any hurt, but bear nobody any ill-will. Prudent care there must be, but not an anxious, perplexing thought; let this care be cast upon God. The disciples of Christ must think more how to do well, than how to speak well. In case of great peril, the disciples of Christ may go out of the way of danger, though they must not go out of the way of duty. No sinful, unlawful means may be used to escape; for then it is not a door of God's opening. The fear of man brings a snare, a perplexing snare, that disturbs our peace; an entangling snare, by which we are drawn into sin; and, therefore, it must be striven and prayed against. Tribulation, distress, and persecution cannot take away God's love to them, or theirs to him. Fear Him, who is able to destroy both soul and body in hell. They must deliver their message publicly, for all are deeply concerned in the doctrine of the gospel. The whole counsel of God must be made known, [Acts.20.27] Ac 20:27. Christ shows them why they should be of good cheer. Their sufferings witnessed against those who oppose his gospel. When God calls us to speak for him, we may depend on him to teach us what to say. A believing prospect of the end of our troubles, will be of great use to support us under them. They may be borne to the end, because the sufferers shall be borne up under them. The strength shall be according to the day. And it is great encouragement to those who are doing Christ's work, that it is a work which shall certainly be done. See how the care of Providence extends to all creatures, even to the sparrows. This should silence all the fears of God's people; Ye are of more value than many sparrows. And the very hairs of your head are all numbered. This denotes the account God takes and keeps of his people. It is our duty, not only to believe in Christ, but to profess that faith, in suffering for him, when we are called to it, as well as in serving him. That denial of Christ only is here meant which is persisted in, and that confession only can have the blessed recompence here promised, which is the real and constant language of faith and love. Religion is worth every thing; all who believe the truth of it, will come up to the price, and make every thing else yield to it. Christ will lead us through sufferings, to glory with him. Those are best prepared for the life to come, that sit most loose to this present life. Though the kindness done to Christ's disciples be ever so small, yet if there be occasion for it, and ability to do no more, it shall be accepted. Christ does not say that they deserve a reward; for we cannot merit any thing from the hand of God; but they shall receive a reward from the free gift of God. Let us boldly confess Christ, and show love to him in all things.
